
### Missing values by column
```{r}
# Display missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(data))
```
If  missing values found, will be replaced. For numeric variables, we use the median, and for categorical variables, we use the most common value. If there are no missing values, no replacement is needed.

```{r}
# Replace missing values in numeric columns with the median
data <- data %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric),
                ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)))

# Replace missing values in categorical columns with the most common value
mode_value <- function(x) {
  ux <- unique(x[!is.na(x)])
  ux[which.max(tabulate(match(x, ux)))]
}

data <- data %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character),
                ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), mode_value(.x), .x)))

# Display missing values after replacement
colSums(is.na(data))
```

### Boxplots to check quantitative-variable outliers

```{r}
# Select numeric variables
numeric_data <- data[, sapply(data, is.numeric)]

# Define different colors
box_colors <- c("yellow", "green", "blue", "orange",
                "red", "purple", "pink", "brown", "cyan")

# Display boxplots
par(mfrow = c(3, 3),
    mar = c(3, 3, 3, 1),
    cex = 0.9)

for (i in 1:ncol(numeric_data)) {
  boxplot(numeric_data[, i],
          main = names(numeric_data)[i],
          col = box_colors[i],
          border = "black",
          horizontal = FALSE,
          ylab = names(numeric_data)[i],
          cex.main = 1,
          cex.lab = 0.9,
          cex.axis = 0.8)
}

# Reset the graph layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1),
    mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2),
    cex = 1)
```

### Summaries and graphs

```{r}
# Count observations for each continent
continent_count <- table(data$continent)

# Make space for the legend
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 8))

# Draw the bar chart
barplot(continent_count,
        main = "Observations by Continent",
        xlab = "Continent",
        ylab = "Number of Observations",
        col = c("yellow", "blue", "green", "orange", "red", "black"),
        border = "Red")

# Add legend on the right
legend("topright",
       inset = c(-0.30, 0),
       legend = names(continent_count),
       fill = c("yellow", "blue", "green", "orange", "red", "purple"),
       title = "Legend",
       xpd = TRUE,
       cex = 0.7)

# Add a single-line frame around the graph
box()

# Restore margins
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 4))

```

### Fill in the exam statement using calculations

```{r}
# Percentage of observations from Europe
europe_percent <- sum(data$continent == "Europe") / nrow(data) * 100

# Count observations with CPI score of 50 or above
cpi_50_count <- sum(data$cpi_score >= 50)

# Average happiness in Europe
europe_mean <- mean(data$happiness_score[data$continent == "Europe"])

# Average happiness in Africa
africa_mean <- mean(data$happiness_score[data$continent == "Africa"])

# Compare Europe's happiness with Africa's
europe_africa_ratio <- europe_mean / africa_mean

# Average happiness in 2015
mean_2015 <- mean(data$happiness_score[data$Year == 2015])

# Average happiness in 2020
mean_2020 <- mean(data$happiness_score[data$Year == 2020])

# Display results
europe_percent
cpi_50_count
europe_mean
africa_mean
europe_africa_ratio
mean_2015
mean_2020
```
### Missing information in the statement:
The EDA shows that `r round(europe_percent, 2)`% of observations come from European countries. Moreover, `r cpi_50_count` out of all country-year observations have a CPI score of 50 or above. In addition, the average happiness score of Europe is `r round(europe_africa_ratio, 2)` times the average happiness score of Africa. Generally, the global average happiness score moved from `r round(mean_2015, 3)` in 2015 to `r round(mean_2020, 3)` in 2020.

### Happiness over time

```{r}
# Average happiness by year
year_happiness <- tapply(data$happiness_score, data$Year, mean)

# Display results
year_happiness

# Draw a line graph
plot(year_happiness,
     type = "b",
     main = "Average Happiness by Year",
     xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Average Happiness Score",
     col = "Red")
```

### Happiness by CPI intervals (10-point groups)

```{r}
# Divide CPI scores into groups of 10
data$cpi_group <- cut(data$cpi_score,
                     breaks = seq(0, 100, 10),
                     labels = c("0-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30-39",
                                "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70-79",
                                "80-89", "90-99"),
                     right = FALSE)

# Calculate average happiness for each CPI group
tapply(data$happiness_score, data$cpi_group, mean)

# Define colors
cpi_colors <- c("yellow", "green", "blue", "orange", "red",
                "purple", "pink", "brown", "gray", "cyan")

# Draw boxplots
boxplot(happiness_score ~ cpi_group,
        data = data,
        main = "Happiness by CPI Group",
        xlab = "CPI Group",
        ylab = "Happiness Score",
        col = cpi_colors,
        las = 2)

# Add legend
legend("topright",
       legend = levels(data$cpi_group),
       fill = cpi_colors,
       title = "CPI Groups",
       cex = 0.7)
```

### CPI and happiness: scatter plot and correlation

```{r}

# Draw a scatter plot
plot(data$cpi_score, data$happiness_score,
     main = "CPI Score and Happiness",
     xlab = "CPI Score (Higher = Less Corruption)",
     ylab = "Happiness Score",
     pch = 19,
     col = "blue")

# Add a regression line
abline(lm(happiness_score ~ cpi_score, data = data),
       col = "red",
       lwd = 2)

# Calculate correlation
cor(data$cpi_score, data$happiness_score)

```

The correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to +1. A positive correlation means that higher CPI scores are generally associated with higher happiness scores. However, correlation does not mean causation.

### Strongly correlated with happiness?

```{r}
# Happiness determinants
determinants <- c("gdp_per_capita", "family", "health",
                  "freedom", "generosity", "government_trust")

# Calculate correlation with happiness
correlations <- numeric(length(determinants))

for (i in 1:length(determinants)) {
  correlations[i] <- cor(data[[determinants[i]]],
                         data$happiness_score)
}

# Display correlations
correlations
names(correlations) <- determinants

# Sort from highest to lowest
sort(correlations, decreasing = TRUE)

# Find the most correlated determinant
determinants[which.max(correlations)]

```

### Identifying low happiness level

```{r}
# Select African countries with CPI scores below 30
low_group <- data[data$continent == "Africa" & data$cpi_score < 30, ]

# List the countries in this group
unique(low_group$Country)

# Count observations in the group
nrow(low_group)

# Calculate average happiness of the group
group_mean <- mean(low_group$happiness_score)

# Calculate global average happiness
global_mean <- mean(data$happiness_score)

# Display the averages
group_mean
global_mean

# Compare the group with the global average
group_mean - global_mean

```

```{r}
# Calculate average happiness for each country
country_mean <- tapply(data$happiness_score, data$Country, mean)

# Sort countries from lowest to highest happiness
sort(country_mean)
```

```{r}
hist(low_group$happiness_score,
     main = "Happiness in African Countries with CPI Below 30",
     xlab = "Happiness Score",
     ylab = "Count",
     col = c("yellow", "green", "blue", "orange", "red", "purple", "pink", "brown"),
     breaks = 15)
```

Compare the group's average happiness with the global average. If the group's average is lower, it means they are less happy on average than the overall population. However, this does not mean that CPI causes the difference

### Five Practical Recommendations for Policymakers

1. Improve the economy: Create jobs, support businesses and improve people's skills to     increase income and living standards.

2. Fight corruption: Promote transparency, accountability and better public services to build trust in government.

3. Improve healthcare: Provide better healthcare services, mental-health support and healthy living conditions.

4. Strengthen social support: Encourage community support, reduce inequality and help vulnerable people.

5. Protect freedom: Promote citizens' rights, participation in decision-making and freedom to make personal choices.

### Conclusion

This analysis examines happiness across countries and over time, and how it relates to CPI and other factors. The results can help policymakers identify areas for improvement, but correlations do not prove causation.
